news.title: Trump Voters Are Giving Republicans a Midterm Warning, Polls Show
news.text: Voters who backed President Donald Trump in 2024 are less enthusiastic about voting in November's midterm elections than those who supported Kamala Harris, recent polls suggest, adding to signs of a turnout challenge for Republicans as they try to hold onto control of Congress. In a Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted September 30 to October 5, 48 percent of Harris's 2024 voters said they were "very enthusiastic" about voting in November, compared with 30 percent of Trump voters. The poll surveyed 4,506 US adults online and had a margin of error of plus or minus 2 percentage points. A separate Economist/YouGov poll found a similar gap using a different question. Asked whether they were more or less enthusiastic about voting this year than in previous congressional election years, 52 percent of Harris's 2024 voters said they were more enthusiastic, compared with 34 percent of Trump's. The YouGov survey was conducted between October 2 and October 5 among 1,513 US adult citizens, including 1,381 registered voters or people who said they had planned to register. The margin of error for registered voters was plus or minus 3.4 percentage points. Democrats Hold a House Edge As Voters Focus on Prices This distinction matters for the midterms, as an enthusiasm gap could affect which party's supporters show up, but it does not confirm how many voters will cast ballots. Meanwhile, a third CBS News/YouGov poll offered a broader look at the potential implications. Its Battleground Tracker estimates Democrats currently have an advantage in the fight for a narrow House majority, citing opposition to the Trump administration's policies and a Republican base that is less likely to turn out. The survey was conducted from September 30 to October 2 among 2,166 US adults and had a margin of error of 2.5 percentage points for the full sample. The House estimate gives the enthusiasm findings added significance. If Republicans have trouble mobilizing their base, that could make it harder to defend their seats. Cost-of-Living Concerns Add to GOP Turnout Challenge Cost of living is also a prominent concern across the polling. In the Reuters/Ipsos survey, 52 percent of respondents said a candidate's position on cost of living would be the most important factor in their congressional vote, including 53 percent of Republicans. The CBS poll also found that many voters felt food and grocery prices were rising and that the administration had not focused enough on lowering costs. It reported that Republicans who thought the administration was not paying enough attention to prices were less likely to say they would definitely vote. For Republicans, the findings suggest a two-part challenge involving addressing an issue voters say matters to their decision and persuading less-motivated supporters that the election is worth turning out for. For Democrats, the polls point to an opportunity if their comparatively higher enthusiasm translates into votes across competitive races. The Reuters/Ipsos poll found other potential signs of Republican vulnerability. Thirteen percent of Trump's 2024 voters said they were unsure who they would support in a congressional election, compared with 7 percent of Harris's voters. Among all respondents who said they were enthusiastic about voting, 62 percent said they were motivated by opposition to Trump, while 36 percent said they were eager to support him. Men, a group Trump won by 12 points in 2024, were more enthusiastic about voting and more certain they would cast a ballot than women in the Reuters/Ipsos poll. Men also favored Democrats over Republicans on the congressional ballot, 43 percent to 39 percent, and had generally favored Republicans in 2025, but since August have leaned back toward the Democrats. Republican strategist Charlie Gerow said the findings raised the stakes for the party's turnout efforts, while predicting the enthusiasm gap could narrow as Republicans focus on the prospect of Democrats gaining power. "The enthusiasm has to be ginned up among Republicans because turnout is what's going to determine the outcome of these midterm elections," Gerow said. Republicans also retain an advantage among voters ages 50 and older, who favored the party by 44 percent to 42 percent in the Reuters/Ipsos poll, though that was down from 8 points in December. Together, the results point to a turnout concern for Republicans. Voters who supported Trump may be less motivated to vote than their Democratic counterparts, while the cost of living is a leading issue and men's preferences have shifted in the generic ballot. The polls, however, do not establish why individual Trump voters feel less enthusiastic, or whether they will ultimately stay home. Both parties are competing for control of Congress in the November 3 midterms. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Sam Stevenson and James Debens
news.summary: Polls show Trump’s 2024 voters are less enthusiastic about the midterms than Harris voters, raising GOP turnout concerns.

news.title: A'ja Wilson wins her third straight WNBA MVP and record fifth overall
news.text: A'ja Wilson fine-tunes her shooting touch following every practice. That little bit of extra work has defined her greatness since being drafted first overall in 2018.On Thursday, she received a voice message from former Vice President Kamala Harris congratulating her on redefining greatness leaguewide after she was named WNBA MVP for a third straight year and for the fifth time overall."Obviously, that is an honor," Wilson said. This one here is just a little bit different, and whatever that may look like, or whatever that may feel, my fifth one, I think, is one that's just ... when you dream as a young girl, your dream so big and you write your goals out, and you just never imagine that you were able to just check them off."And when you're able to check them off — small wins, big wins — it truly means a lot. And so I think that's why I cried a little bit harder on this one, because 15-year-old A'ja wasn't sitting up here dreaming about being a five-time MVP. She wasn't dreaming about being a three-time champion. She was dreaming about surviving this world."The 30-year-old Wilson once again led the league in scoring (26.2) while shooting nearly 53% from the field. She averaged 9.4 rebounds, a career-best 3.2 assists and 1.9 blocks.Wilson has the defending champion Aces back in the WNBA semifinals for the eighth consecutive season, although Las Vegas is down 2-0 in the best-of-five series against Golden State. Minnesota's Olivia Miles received six first-place votes and 40 second-place votes (442 points), while Indiana guards Kelsey Mitchell and Caitlin Clark followed with 287 and 212 points, respectively.No WNBA player besides Wilson has more than three MVPs, with Sheryl Swoopes, Lisa Leslie and Lauren Jackson each having a trio. On the NBA side, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar had six and Michael Jordan and Bill Russell each had five."A'ja Wilson is one of one," Fargas said. "She's now standing in a category that no other WNBA player in the history of the league has accomplished. She's in the conversations with the Michael Jordans and the Wayne Gretzkys of the world — where she belongs."

news.title: CNN Data Guru Floored by Trump’s ‘Laughably Bad’ Crisis
news.text:
President Donald Trump’s approval numbers are “laughably bad,” according to CNN data analyst Harry Enten, who warned that no president in modern history has faced a worse position this close to Election Day.

New polling from the Pew Research Center shows Trump’s net approval rating is an astonishing 38 points underwater. The figures triggered disbelief on air as analysts examined the mounting electoral crisis threatening the administration’s legislative agenda and the Republican Party’s congressional majorities.

“No president I’ve ever seen is in a worse position before a midterm election than President Trump,” Enten said. “You go all the way back. You go back to Harry S. Truman, FDR. At this point before a midterm, ever, ever, ever... the worst I’ve ever seen is Donald John Trump, 38 points underwater.”

Enten stressed that the Pew figures are not an outlier, pointing to a string of major national surveys showing virtually identical results. 

Trump is 33 points underwater according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll, following an earlier Ipsos survey that placed him at a 34-point deficit. Matching Pew’s record-low benchmark, an Associated Press survey and a CNN poll also show the president 38 points and 34 points underwater, respectively.

“No other president before a midterm election was even at minus 31,” Enten noted. “We are looking at history in the making here for the unpopularity of President Trump.”

The historical comparison underscores the severe political friction awaiting Republicans down the ballot. “It’s historic headwinds in which you are essentially going, ‘Oh my God, how am I supposed to win with numbers from a president this bad?’” Enten said.

The sharpest decline for the administration comes from independent voters, who split evenly between Trump and former Vice President Kamala Harris during the 2024 presidential contest. Current survey data shows Trump’s standing with independents has plummeted to 57 points underwater. 

“You just never see numbers” like that, Enten said, adding that he struggled to find adjectives adequate to describe the plunge.

The analyst also pointed to Trump’s explicit push for supporters to “vote like I’m on the ballot” during midterm campaigning.

“Democrats, please, pretty, pretty, please, with a cherry on top, they are saying, yes, vote as if President Trump is on the ballot,” Enten said. “Because if he is on the ballot, you can pretty much guarantee that Democrats will take back the United States House.”

He added that the president’s low standing directly explains why Democratic prospects for capturing the United States Senate have continued to climb.

“This president, as unpopular as he is, is dragging Republicans underwater,” Enten said.

news.title: US Polling ‘Nostradamus’ Predicts Which Senate Seats Democrats Will Flip
news.text: Historian and political forecaster Allan Lichtman has predicted that Democrats will take control of the U.S. Senate in November’s midterm elections, forecasting that five Republican-held seats will flip to the Democrats. Lichtman, dubbed the “Nostradamus” of U.S. election forecasting, expects Democrats to hold Michigan and New Hampshire as well as winning North Carolina, Maine, Ohio, Texas and Alaska. His forecast would give Democrats 52 Senate seats against 44 Republicans, with the remaining seats held by independents. Republicans currently hold 53 seats in the 100-member Senate, compared with 45 Democrats and two independents who caucus with Democrats, giving Republicans a 53-47 advantage in party alignment. In a video outlining his predictions, Lichtman pointed to growing dissatisfaction with President Donald Trump, strong Democratic enthusiasm and the party’s performance in recent special elections. But do polling and prediction markets support his ambitious forecast? Newsweek contacted Lichtman's team via online form on Friday for comment. North Carolina: Lichtman’s Strongest Pick Lichtman describes North Carolina as the surest Democratic pickup, arguing that Republicans have withdrawn funding from the race. RealClearPolling’s average of surveys conducted up to October 8 put Democratic former Governor Roy Cooper at 50 percent and Republican Michael Whatley at 43 percent. Kalshi's market listing gave Cooper a 96.5 percent chance of winning, compared with 3.5 percent for Whatley. Both indicators strongly favor Cooper, making North Carolina the most convincing of Lichtman’s five predictions based on those figures. Maine: Can Democrats Defeat Susan Collins? Lichtman predicts Republican Senator Susan Collins will lose despite her history of winning competitive elections. A polling average last updated October 1 put Democrat Troy Jackson at 48.4 percent and Collins at 46.6 percent. A Washington Post-Schar School poll published October 9 found Jackson leading 50 percent to 46 percent. Kalshi’s market listing gave Jackson about a 66 percent chance of winning, against 34 percent for Collins. The figures favor Democrats, but the narrow polling lead suggests the race remains competitive. Ohio: Sherrod Brown’s Comeback Bid Lichtman expects Democratic former Senator Sherrod Brown to defeat Republican incumbent Jon Husted, arguing that Brown’s appeal to working-class voters could help him overcome Ohio’s Republican lean. A CNN poll updated October 8 put Brown at 45 percent and Husted at 43 percent. Kalshi’s market listing gave Brown a 62 percent chance of victory, compared with 38 percent for Husted. Texas: Potential Democratic Breakthrough Lichtman believes Democratic state Representative James Talarico could defeat Republican state Attorney General Ken Paxton, pointing to Paxton’s controversies and Trump’s declining approval ratings. RealClearPolling’s average of surveys conducted up to October 8 put Talarico and Paxton neck and neck at 45 percent. Kalshi’s market listing gave Talarico a 65 percent chance of winning, against 35 percent for Paxton. The figures suggest Democrats have a credible opportunity, but a victory would still represent a major breakthrough in a state that has favored Republicans. Alaska: Close Race With Democrats Favored Lichtman predicts that Democratic former Representative Mary Peltola will defeat Republican Senator Dan Sullivan, despite Alaska’s Republican-leaning voting history. RealClearPolling’s average of surveys updated October 7 put Peltola at 51 percent and Sullivan at 49 percent. Kalshi’s market listing was more optimistic, giving the Democrat a 75 percent chance of winning, compared with 25 percent for the Republican. Lichtman’s 2024 Prediction Raises Questions Lichtman’s Senate forecast comes after his high-profile failure to predict the 2024 presidential election correctly. He forecast that Kamala Harris would defeat Donald Trump, who ultimately won. Lichtman is best known for his Keys to the White House system, which uses political and economic indicators to forecast presidential elections. However, he says his Senate predictions are based on his experience and understanding of American politics rather than a formal model. He also identified South Carolina, Iowa, Kansas and Nebraska as potential additional opportunities for Democrats, although those states are not central to his forecast. Lichtman argued that Trump’s unpopularity could hurt Republican candidates in multiple states. The polling and market figures offer some support for his predictions, particularly in North Carolina, while the other races remain more competitive. His forecast is a bold prediction of a Democratic wave. Whether Democrats can flip all five seats and secure the 52-seat majority that he expects will depend on turnout, individual candidates and how accurately polls capture voter preferences. news.summary: Allan Lichtman predicts Democrats will flip five Senate seats in 2026, potentially reshaping control of Congress.

news.text:
Hello, all, and welcome to Friday, Oct. 9, 2026 — the start of Columbus Day weekend, so the mail won't run Monday and the banks will be closed. Plan accordingly.

My calendar says it's Leif Erikson Day, International Beer and Pizza Day, World Egg Day, World Post Day, Moldy Cheese Day, Curious Events Day, Fire Prevention Day, and Sneakers Day. So toast Leif Erikson with a beer and an egg-topped pizza, mail a thank-you note to your letter carrier, and lace up the sneakers before the fire marshal sees what the moldy cheese did to your fridge.

Today in History:

1000: Leif Erikson is believed to have landed in North America, possibly in what is now Newfoundland.1635: Massachusetts Bay Colony banishes religious dissident Roger Williams, who goes on to found Rhode Island.1701: The Collegiate School of Connecticut, later Yale University, receives its charter.1825: The sloop Restauration lands in New York Harbor with 52 Norwegian Quakers, the first organized immigration from Norway.1874: Representatives of 22 countries sign the Treaty of Bern, creating the General Postal Union, today's Universal Postal Union.1888: The Washington Monument opens to the public.1930: Laura Ingalls becomes the first woman to fly solo across the continent, hopping from New York to California in nine stops.1936: The first generator at Hoover Dam begins sending electricity to Los Angeles. There are 17 cranking out power there today, plus two backups, but there's water level problems at Lake Mead. If the water levels fall another few feet, nine of those 17 will shut down.1975: Soviet scientist Andrei Sakharov wins the Nobel Peace Prize.1985: The hijackers of the Italian cruise ship Achille Lauro surrender in Port Said, Egypt, two days after seizing the ship.1992: A meteorite smashes into a family's car in a Peekskill, N.Y., driveway. How'd you like to have been in on the phone call to the Insurance people?2004: Afghanistan holds its first direct presidential election.2006: North Korea announces it has conducted its first nuclear test.2012: Taliban gunmen shoot 15-year-old Malala Yousafzai for advocating girls' education in Pakistan.

Birthdays Today include: Camille Saint-Saëns, composer; Charles R. Walgreen, drugstore chain founder; John Lennon, singer-songwriter (The Beatles); Brian Lamb, C-SPAN founder; Jackson Browne, singer ("Running on Empty," "Take It Easy"); Tony Shalhoub, actor (Men in Black, Monk); and Mike Singletary, Hall of Fame linebacker.

I wrote at some length yesterday about the worldwide swing to the populist right. If you missed it, start there, because today’s argument builds on one paragraph in particular:

I would call what we’re seeing a worldwide gag reflex. A gag reflex is triggered by whatever you’re choking on, and gagging is nature’s way of solving the problem. It isn’t a philosophy. It’s an immune response. Trump and the end of USAID didn’t cause this one. Voters are reacting to what the worldwide Left has tried to force down their throats.

Today, I’m taking that a step further. Donald Trump didn’t create this response. He’s part of it, a symptom of a much larger reaction, not its cause. That’s why I keep saying MAGA won’t end with Trump, because it didn't start with him, either. Indeed, it’s just getting started.

I know what’s clogging social media. The Left has a comforting little mantra that they're spreading like fertilizer. "When Trump leaves, MAGA goes with him." Isn’t that convenient? All they have to do is wait for one man to leave the stage, and the inconvenient voters will come to their senses, apologize, and resume voting for the people who made them angry in the first place.

Sure. And the next time your smoke alarm goes off, just pull the battery. Problem solved. No need to investigate the smoke, let alone the fire.

That attitude confuses the man who gave a movement its most recognizable face with the reasons millions of people joined it. But to extend the analogy I painted yesterday, an immune response doesn’t stand down because one white blood cell retires.

The movement was already on the road before Trump got behind the wheel. I went into this in some detail yesterday. We call these worldwide movements “Trumpian” because Trump is the familiar face and the one the progressives love to hate. 

The chronology, though, says otherwise. The Tea Party wave of 2010 gave Republicans 63 House seats, the biggest midterm swing since 1938, six years before Trump won the presidency. Germany’s AfD was founded in 2013. Britain voted for Brexit in 2016, and both happened before Trump won anything. In Latin America, Bukele took office in 2019, Chaves in 2022, and Milei in 2023, long before Trump’s return, as Sarah Anderson argued.

Understand me here: Trump didn’t manufacture this wave; he surfed it. And because he’s the best-known surfer in the lineup, people started confusing his name with the ocean. In fact, MAGA existed and was growing rapidly before Trump even renamed it. It's just that he was smart enough to identify it and stand in front of it.

If MAGA were a personality cult that needed him in the Oval Office for its survival, you’d expect it to have withered while he was out. In September 2022, almost two years after he left, 38% of Republicans still identified as MAGA, the Economist/YouGov poll reported. By May 2026, it was 62%. Some of that growth came as he returned to power, so I won’t claim the numbers prove independence. What they show is a base that was there before the return.

Is it the whole country? No. It’s about a quarter of adults. But a quarter of the country and a majority of one of its two parties isn’t a fringe that evaporates on a schedule regardless of any fantasy being offered by the progressives. 

Oh, and as for the future, look at who’s lined up for ‘28. At CPAC in March, Vance took 53% in the straw poll and Rubio 35%. CNN, which is always ready to pee on the GOP’s parade, is careful to note the straw poll isn’t scientific, and Vance slipped from 61% last year. But he still leads every recent 2028 primary poll, and Rubio has said he’d back Vance if he runs. The fight inside the party is over who carries the torch, not whether anybody does. And these are a couple of very strong candidates.

Remember, too, that the rest of the world is running the same script. Jair Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year sentence. His son Flávio finished first in Brazil’s opening round, about 47% to Lula’s 45%, and they meet in a runoff Oct. 25. In France, Marine Le Pen’s embezzlement conviction was upheld on appeal in July, though the court cut her ban and she says she’s running. Even so, the National Rally had Jordan Bardella ready, and an April poll had him marginally ahead of her, 34% to 32%. And Argentina: Juan Perón was born Oct. 8, 1895, and died in 1974. Peronism shaped Argentine politics for decades after, until voters picked Javier Milei in 2023. And the rest of the world sees the huge turnaround there.

Related: It's Not Just South America: The Worldwide Move to the Right

No movement gets a lifetime warranty. But none of these folded when its founder left the stage. MAGA won't, either.

And before you start, yes, the Democrats are currently leading the polls. I’m not going to insult you by pretending otherwise. Nate Silver’s average has Democrats up about nine on the generic ballot, but not quite as generous across the specific candidates, and one prediction market gives them a 64% chance of a sweep.

Thing is, I don’t really care. That seems a bold statement to make, until you realize that polls have a record. They’re all available on the net these days. The pollsters’ own trade group found 2020’s national polls overstated Biden’s margin by 3.9 points, and Pew says 2024’s errors ran in the same direction, only smaller. Discount accordingly. Are the polls wrong? isn’t even a question anymore, given the last few cycles.

Let's remember that the pollsters were all predicting a Kamala Harris win. You may recall how that worked out.And yes, the numbers being reported currently, even with that four-point or so discount, don't line up to a GOP victory. But think, now: With this much on the line, does anyone with at least two working brain cells figure the leftists are going to get more honest? Spoiler alert: not me. Then, too, they didn't have the DSA splitting the ticket in the last few cycles. They certainly do now. With the races as close as they've been, that is a huge impact. 

Even assuming a loss (which I seriously doubt), we need to understand that losing an election isn’t the same as losing a movement. Republicans lost the White House in 2012, and by 2014 they had their biggest House majority since 1928 and the Senate. Two years later came Trump. The grievances against the progressives won’t leave when Trump does. The crime, the migration, the prices, and the sense that elites stopped listening predate him, and they’ll outlast him. The movement survives only if it delivers. If Republicans lose in November, the answer isn’t to blame the polls. It’s to ask what voters wanted and what the party failed to deliver. That comes back to the Establishment GOP.

It comes down to this: The gag reflex I spoke of yesterday doesn’t care which party is holding the spoon. It reacts to what’s being forced down the public’s throat. So, the answer to all of this is to show up. Pay attention. Check the claims. And if you believe, as I do, that MAGA has a future, don’t assume somebody else will carry it for you. Act. Get your buns to the booths. Period. Full stop.

Thought for the Day: My reference to the Hoover Dam sends the message clearly: The dam doesn't make the power; the pressure behind it does. Be the pressure that makes the power.

Take care, gang. And you might wanna say a prayer for the folks in Alabama and Florida, and for the TV and radio people having to try to pronounce "Isaias." Hopefully, I'll see you tomorrow.

news.title: Mortgages Hit 3-Year High: How Payments Have Risen Under Trump
news.text: U.S. mortgage rates have climbed to their highest level in nearly three years, adding to affordability pressures for homebuyers as the cost of living emerges as a key issue ahead of November's midterm elections. The average rate on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage reached 7.40 percent for the week ending October 8, according to Freddie Mac, as reported by Realtor.com, marking the seventh consecutive weekly increase. Rates rose from 7.28 percent the previous week and are now well above the 6.30 percent recorded a year ago. "These elevated mortgage rates have the housing market spooked," says Realtor.com senior economist Joel Berner. The latest increase comes amid inflation concerns, a global bond market sell-off and worries about rising government deficits. Federal Reserve officials have also indicated that further interest rate increases may be necessary to bring inflation under control. Newsweek contacted the National Association of Realtors on Friday via email for comment. For Americans hoping to buy a home, rising borrowing costs present another obstacle in a market already made difficult by elevated property prices. How Much Have Average Mortgage Rates Changed Since Trump Took Office? When President Trump took office in January 2025, the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate was 6.91 percent, according to a report by Freddie Mac. As of September 2026, a typical U.S. home had a median listing price of $419,250, according to data from Federal Reserve and Realtor.com. Assuming that a buyer is purchasing a typical U.S. home taking on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage with a 20 percent down payment, they are now paying an average of $246 more per month, or around $2,954 more per year than they were last year. Overall, compared to when Trump took office, they are now paying $111 more per month, or approximately $1,333 more per year, in principal and interest on their mortgage, assuming the same home price of $419,250 and a 20 percent down payment. How Mortgage Rates Affect Buyers Higher mortgage rates mean buyers pay more to finance the same property, even when its purchase price remains unchanged. The increase can push monthly payments beyond what many households can comfortably afford, forcing prospective buyers to consider cheaper homes or delay purchasing altogether. Mortgage rates are influenced by several factors, including longer-term Treasury yields and expectations about inflation. They do not move directly in line with the Federal Reserve's benchmark rate, although expectations of tighter monetary policy can put additional pressure on borrowing costs. The housing market has already shown signs of strain. Pending home sales fell year over year in August and September, while some sellers have been forced to reduce asking prices to attract buyers, according to Realtor.com. Although increased housing inventory and softer prices may give buyers more negotiating power, those benefits can be offset by higher financing costs. Higher rates can also discourage existing homeowners from selling. Those with mortgages secured at substantially lower rates may be reluctant to move if doing so means taking out a more expensive loan, potentially limiting the supply of properties available to buyers. Cost of Living Looms Over Midterms The mortgage increase comes as affordability concerns weigh on the political outlook for Republicans ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. A Reuters/Ipsos poll published October 8 found that the cost of living was the top issue on Americans' minds as they considered how to vote, ahead of democratic values and immigration. The poll also highlighted a gap in enthusiasm between supporters of President Donald Trump and those who backed former Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 election. Some 48 percent of Harris voters said they were very enthusiastic about voting in November, compared with 30 percent of Trump voters. Trump's approval rating stood at 32 percent, matching a record low previously recorded in September, Reuters reported. Housing costs add to the financial pressures facing households. Mortgage payments are among the largest regular expenses many Americans face, and rising borrowing costs can leave families with less money for other essentials. Although mortgage rates are influenced by bond markets, inflation expectations and Federal Reserve policy rather than presidential decisions alone, housing affordability remains part of the broader economic picture voters may use to judge the administration. Will Rates Fall Again? The near-term outlook for mortgage rates remains uncertain. Persistent inflation concerns and rising Treasury yields have pushed borrowing costs higher, while the prospect of further monetary tightening could create additional pressure. Buyers hoping for lower rates may therefore face a difficult choice between purchasing now and waiting for financing conditions to improve. Waiting could bring lower borrowing costs, but future rates are not guaranteed to fall, and home prices may also change. For now, the latest rise adds another challenge for Americans trying to enter the housing market. With cost of living a leading concern for voters, the affordability of homeownership could remain an important issue as Americans head to the polls in November. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Matthew Robinson and Trevor Davies
news.summary: The average rate on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage reached 7.40 percent for the week ending October 8, according to Freddie Mac.

news.title: Stop talking about the US ‘Jewish vote’. It's not that simple | Judith Levine
news.text:
Everybody wants the Jewish vote. As if there were one. Jews are educated, generally liberal. Although they comprise only about 2% of the electorate, they vote in high numbers, overwhelmingly for Democrats. In 2024, 79% chose Kamala Harris. They are also assumed to be steadfast friends of Israel, no matter what it does. Republicans, waging a fake war on antisemitism while courting white supremacists, consider Jews increasingly up for grabs.

Nationally, Jewish Americans are concentrated in a few bright blue spots. A 2020 map from the Jewish Electorate Institute showed a third of Jews living in 20 congressional districts – out of 435 – most of them in New York, New Jersey, California and (purple) Florida. Of these, only one sent a Republican to Washington.

Today, it’s two. Florida’s 21st district switched parties only after falling victim to redistricting in 2022. The other outlier has elected the pro-Israel, anti-immigration Republican Chris Smith every term since 1981. Why? The mapmakers’ explanation: New Jersey fourth district includes Lakewood, where half the residents are ultra-Orthodox – scrupulously, ceaselessly observant. Unsurprisingly, among white voters, regular religious service attendance is a big predictor of conservatism.

In other words, in Lakewood, Orthodox may be more salient that Jewish.

In fact, if pro-Israel candidates are looking for votes, even Jewish is no longer salient. White Evangelical Christians are more firmly supportive of Israel than American Jews. The US is home to the largest population of Christian Zionists in the world, numbering more than 30 million, a third of whom belong to Christians United for Israel, the largest Zionist organization is the US.

The Bible belt churches these people attend preach that the founding of Israel in 1948 was part of God’s plan to bring about the End Times, and the ongoing hostilities in the Middle East are the mayhem and destruction preceding the second coming of Christ (when nonbelievers – including Jews – will drown in the Lake of Fire).

While the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac) spends far more on political campaigns, Christians United for Israel is busy mobilizing its millions to grassroots action.

Meanwhile, a minority of American Jews now call themselves Zionists. A late-2025 Washington Post poll found that six in 10 believed Israel was committing war crimes in Gaza; four in 10 said the assault was genocide. And aside from the fiercest partisans, for many young Jews, Israel just isn’t that important.

The Gaza war figured large in the 2024 presidential elections, as the civilian death toll mounted and the Biden-Harris administration stood unwaveringly beside Israel. Now, even as the killing spreads to the West Bank and southern Lebanon, US voters are moving on. Affordability is the winning buzzword this cycle, at least for Democrats. Almost no one is thinking about foreign policy.

What about abortion? Climate change? Voting rights? The press, the pundits, and the mainstream party strategists keep behaving as if every Jew cares about Israel – and all Jews care about is Israel – and a candidate must be pro-Zionist or lose the elusive Jewish vote.

We saw this during the campaign of the New York mayor, Zohran Mamdani. Forthright support for Palestinian self-determination had long been central to his politics, and to his appeal to progressives. But Mamdani was running for mayor, not president. His brilliant stroke was affordability – a theme that is easily understandable, widely relatable, and capable of making socialist solutions sound reasonable.

Nevertheless, from the moment he appeared, the press, from the New York Times op-ed page to college newspapers to the international Jewish press, made the election a referendum on Israel – and, more perniciously, on Islam.

Mamdani’s Democratic primary opponent, former governor Andrew Cuomo, attacked him with flagrant Islamophobia, conflating his critique of Israel with antisemitism and signalling that his faith was a danger to Jews.

The fearmongering did not defeat Mamdani.

In the end, only a third of Jews voted for him; in Hasidic neighborhoods, 90% went for Cuomo. But progressive Jewish organizations including Jewish Voice for Peace and Jews for Racial and Economic Justice endorsed him. He won in almost every racial and class demographic and pulled in three-quarters of voters under 30.

What’s the lesson here? The youth vote – plus the Black vote, the Hispanic vote, the working-class vote, etc – plus good ideas and a great campaign put Mamdani over the top. Furthermore, an analysis by Good Authority concludes that no position on Israel, pro or con, is driving Jews out of the Democratic party.

Now Abdul El-Sayed, the Muslim Democrat running for Senate in Michigan, is shlepping the burden of this vaguely defined, perpetually disgruntled “Jewish vote”. After narrowly winning the primary, he apologized to members of the Jewish community for a statement he made after a Lebanese-born naturalized citizen rammed his truck into a large synagogue, injuring a guard.

The apology came after El-Sayed clumsily linked the man’s antisemitism to Israeli violence in Lebanon, saying: “Hurt people hurt people.” It was an inoffensive adage among, say, prison abolitionists. But to some Jews, it sounded as if El-Sayed felt more sympathy for the perpetrator than for his targeted victims.

The Republicans have taken advantage of these fissures, attacking El-Sayed with a combination of Islamophobia and the usual hypocritical condemnations of antisemitism. At their midterm “convention”, El-Sayed’s opponent Mike Rogers claimed, falsely, that the Democrat had ties to the Muslim Brotherhood. And while El-Sayed definitively distanced himself from the leftwing Israel critic Hasan Piker – a Twitch streamer the press began to cover obsessively – speaker after speaker hammered on the connection between the two men.

These tactics appear to be falling flat. A recent New York Times/Siena poll found that most Michiganders have never heard of Piker. The poll found that El-Sayed leads his opponent by 39 points among voters 44 and younger, who are far more critical of Israel’s policies than their elders. That generational split is also pronounced among Jews.

El-Sayed has the endorsements of JVP and IfNotNow, an organization that attracts many young Jews who are painfully rejecting their parents’ Zionism, as well as Vermont’s Jewish senator, Bernie Sanders. While Rogers has been collecting pledges of votes from Jewish Michiganders, more than 600 “Michigan Jews for Democracy”, including elected officials and rabbis, have signed a letter in support of El-Sayed.

Recently, Mamdani repeated his condemnation of Benjamin Netanyahu as a war criminal who should be arrested in advance of the Israeli prime minister’s visit to New York to address the UN. That revived Zionist fury toward the mayor, but Jews both supportive and critical of Israel – and Mamdani – held noisy rallies.

The reason for Mamdani to keep trying to speak to both sides is not to win the mythical Jewish vote. It is to make common cause with people who don’t want Israel swept into the sea but also cannot abide a Jewish ethnostate whose survival depends on occupation and apartheid.

That said, if El-Sayed were the Islamist Jew-hater his enemies claim he is, it should be obvious to a lot more Jews. If it were obvious to a lot more Jews, Aipac would not have had to pour $32m – unsuccessfully – into Stevens’ campaign or contemplate pouring more into supporting Rogers in the general election.

And of course, the “Arab American” or “Muslim vote” is no more unanimous than the hypothetical Jewish vote.

To be frank, the whole discourse stinks. It boils down to “support the Muslim” or “support the Jew”, as if this were some ancient racial animosity – natural enemies “fighting”, as Trump said of the Palestinians and Israeli Jews, “for a thousand years”.

Not only is this contention untrue. Such thinking obviates politics, the effort to understand a problem and convince others that your solution is best. It is not good for the Jews – or for anyone. And it is deadly for a secular, pluralistic democracy.

 Judith Levine is a frequent contributor to the Guardian. Her Substack is Today in Fascism

news.text:
Why is populism, broadly defined, on the brink of historic victories around the world, while populism in the form of President Donald Trump’s Republican Party is poised to lose one or both houses of Congress in the United States?

The troubles Trump’s Republicans face are not a mystery. It was always unlikely that Republicans would maintain their hair’s-breadth House majority.But the 2026 lineup of Senate seats looked favorable, with only one Republican defending a seat in a state Kamala Harris carried and all but one defending seats in states Trump carried by double digits in 2024. At least two Democrats were defending seats in states Trump carried in 2024, and retirements opened up two other seats in marginal states.

That picture has now changed. Persistent inflation, some of it plausibly triggered by Trump’s tariffs, has hurt Republicans. Democrats have sprinted to big polling leads in Georgia and North Carolina, and various combinations of weak Republicans and strong Democrats have left Republicans trailing in Alaska, Iowa, Ohio and Texas — states Trump carried by double digits two years ago.

Democrats are already planning investigations of Trump’s financial shenanigans and drafting articles of impeachment. They have high hopes of a 2028 trifecta: the House, Senate and presidency. Republicans’ trifecta hopes are clouded by the prospect of primaries pitting Trump supporters against his opponents.

What a different picture in the rest of the world. Populist veteran Marine Le Pen is the frontrunner for president of France next year, while next month’s snap election in Spain is likely to put the populist Vox party into a governing coalition.

Germany’s populist AfD just won the state election in Saxony-Anhalt, and it’s getting hard to imagine how the traditional parties can keep excluding it from federal coalitions. Italy’s Giorgia Meloni, with roots in a populist party that had been excluded from power for years, heads the longest-serving government in post-World War II Italy.

Britain’s populist Reform UK party has lost its lead in public polls after the Labour government ditched Keir Starmer and installed Andy Burnham as prime minister. But it’s interesting that Labour, founded in 1900, felt obliged to reach beyond the usual parliamentary leadership ranks to select first a professional barrister and then a regional mayor. Reform UK, founded in 2018, is still polling ahead of the Conservatives, whose roots go back to 1846.

The picture is even starker in the Western Hemisphere. In November 2023, free-market booster Javier Milei defeated the Peronist candidate in Argentina after attacking high inflation and bloated bureaucracy. In the 15 months beginning in April 2025, conservative populists defeated leftist candidates in Ecuador, Bolivia, Chile, Peru and Colombia.

In the first round of elections this past Sunday in Brazil, Flavio Bolsonaro led incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva 47% to 45%. Bolsonaro’s father, Jair, now confined to house arrest, was elected in 2018 and lost in 2022 to Lula, as he is usually called, 51% to 49%. Lula was previously elected in 2002 and 2006, and his Workers’ Party has won five of the last six presidential elections. He was leading in preelection polls, but Flavio Bolsonaro is considered likely, though not certain, to win the Oct. 25 runoff.

What accounts for the populist wave? In Europe, many voters have recoiled against high levels of immigration, especially of young Muslim men, amid worries that they are not assimilating economically or culturally. Bloated government payrolls and high rates of violent crime are populist complaints in both Europe and South America.

The populist complaint, voiced in loud and raucous terms, is that established parties in government have not just failed to solve these problems but have refused to do so. They have cordoned off populist parties and candidates, as if opposing open borders for immigrants who are difficult to assimilate or supporting tough sentences for violent criminals were morally equivalent to Nazi or communist mass murder.

So how do we explain why populism is on the rise beyond the U.S., even as it seems mired in failure here?

One explanation is that Trumpism is not really mired in failure. Trump has been president of the U.S. for almost six of the last 10 years and has had substantial policy successes. They range from economic growth exceeding that of other major countries to the recent treaty promising American control of Greenland.

That success is part of his problem. After three and a half years of the Biden administration arguing that the law left it no alternative to an open-door immigration policy, the second Trump administration has proved that the border can be controlled.

This success signals to a future administration that it will pay a steep price if it returns to open borders. But for the moment, voters no longer need a Trumpist to close the border. It’s been done.

And, given the messiness of everyday life, it’s been done with some collateral damage to the populist cause. Consider the heavy-handed Immigration and Customs Enforcement raids in Minneapolis choreographed by the oddball Homeland Security appointee Kristi Noem and her consigliere, Corey Lewandowski.

There is something in the nature of populist politics — the willingness to take on and persevere against established media, corporate, academic and party elites — that produces a peculiarly personal kind of leadership. Success in ignoring hoary shibboleths only encourages such leaders to defy warnings they would be better off heeding.

Populist politics has given us the family dramas of the Trumps in America, the Le Pens in France, and the Bolsonaros in Brazil. It has given America a president who threatens the sovereignty of friendly or largely unoffending allies such as Canada and Denmark.

It has saddled the Republican Party with inflation imposed by tariffs for which there is no perceptible demand from even the smallest subgroup of the electorate. Yet Trump supplies them in abundance, driven by idiosyncratic theories he concocted in the 1980s.

The president’s party has suffered as well from his choice of suboptimal Republican nominees, which has already cost Republicans several Senate seats and seems on the verge of, amazingly, costing them a Senate seat in Texas as well. A leader who has gotten where he is by defying conventional wisdom that proves wrong gets into the habit of defying it even when, as on many occasions, it is absolutely right.

From time to time, we hear predictions from politicians, both populist and conventional, that their side will govern for the next generation. That seldom happens. The Democratic Party won House majorities in every election from 1954 through 1992. But Republicans held the presidency for 26 of those 40 years, and Democrats were usually split between Southern conservatives and Northern liberals.

In the 32 years since 1994, presidential elections have produced party trifectas — majorities in both houses of Congress and control of the presidency -- in six of eight election years. But only once did a trifecta last as long as four years, and in one case, it ended after five months. Populist movements can achieve worthy goals spurned by more conventional forces. But they are subject to the rules that every person’s strength is also his weakness and that, in human affairs, success tends to breed failure.COPYRIGHT 2026 CREATORS.COM

news.title: Will Indian-American voters who supported Trump in 2024 return to Democrats in the US midterms?
news.text:
Pre-election polls in 2024 showed that between 25% and 31% of Indian American voters intended to support Donald Trump, who went on to defeat Vice President Kamala Harris, the first major-party presidential nominee of Indian descent.
With the midterm elections less than a month away, a key question is whether Trump and the Republicans can retain the level of support they attracted from Indian Americans two years ago — or whether some of those voters will return to the Democratic Party, which has historically enjoyed overwhelming support among the community.
A February 2026 survey by the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace offered a more complicated picture. Although Indian Americans remained predominantly Democratic, the party's identification among the community had declined from 52% in 2020 to 46% in 2026. Republican identification stood at 19% while 29% identified as independents.
The survey also found that Trump’s support among Indian American men under 40 had fallen from 40% in 2024 to 24% in early 2026, suggesting that some of the gains he made among younger voters may have eroded.
The findings underscore a central uncertainty heading into November: whether dissatisfaction with Trump will translate into renewed Democratic support or leave more Indian American voters politically independent.
It’s the economy, stupid
Recent national polling suggests that parts of the electoral coalition Trump assembled in 2024 are under strain amid concerns about gas prices, inflation, the conflict with Iran and the administration’s restrictive immigration policies.
For Indian Americans, those concerns are compounded by an anti-H-1B campaign led by some of Trump's far-right allies, accompanied by growing hostility toward Indian immigrants and the broader community.
Whether these pressures translate into changes in voting patterns will become clearer on November 3.
Early ballot-request data from several key states suggest strong Democratic engagement in several states, although the figures offer limited insight into how voters will ultimately cast their ballots.
In Pennsylvania, Democrats account for 66% of ballot requests, while in Iowa, their share has risen to 67%, up from 54% in the previous election. In North Carolina, Democrats account for 42% of requests, compared with 36% two years ago.
Although ballot choices remain secret until votes are counted, the figures suggest heightened enthusiasm among Democratic voters. Whether that translates into an electoral advantage remains to be seen.
Amit Jani, managing partner at political consulting firm JD Advisory Group, who previously served in the Obama and Biden administrations and at the US Department of Homeland Security, cautioned against reading too much into the early voting trends.
“From several current indicators, including voter enthusiasm and historical midterm voting patterns, Democrats have reasons for optimism heading into the midterm elections,” he said. “But early voting data should be interpreted cautiously: party registration and ballot-request data can tell us something about enthusiasm and participation, but they do not tell us how those voters actually cast their ballots.”
Political analysts are closely watching emerging voting patterns, while some community leaders report growing interest in the midterms among Indian Americans.
Virginia, which voted decisively for Harris in 2024, offers one indication of heightened voter participation. As of October 7, 2026, a total of 448,933 ballots had been cast in the state, compared with 236,405 at the same point in 2022.
With roughly 175,000 Indian Americans accounting for about 2% of Virginia's population, the increase raises questions about whether the community is participating in the broader surge in electoral activity.
However, the statewide figures do not establish whether Indian American turnout has increased or which party those voters favour.
Neha Dewan, national co-director of South Asians for America, an advocacy organisation working to elect South Asian American candidates across the United States, offered a measured assessment of the early voting numbers.
“Democrats tend to vote early, as they did in 2024, when former vice president Harris still lost. Polling has also become less reliable, so the results here deserve close attention,” she said.
Dewan, whose organisation was founded five years ago to strengthen South Asian American political engagement and influence, acknowledged growing political interest among Indian Americans, though it remains unclear whether that enthusiasm favors either party.
“South Asians feel the energy of this cycle on both sides of the aisle. Many South Asians are running for office this year at the local, state, and federal levels,” she said.
“On the Republican side, Vivek Ramaswamy's run for governor of Ohio excites some in our community, even though the party's agenda on immigration and civil rights does not reflect the values most Indian Americans hold. For these voters, the significance of an Indian American winning high office appears to drive their support.”
On the Democratic side, Dewan highlighted two congressional candidates generating considerable interest: Dr. Amish Shah in Arizona and Pia Dandiya in Florida.
“Both are running in flippable districts, and both are engaging the Indian American community in record numbers,” she said.
What about Trump’s relationship with India?
Another factor shaping Indian American political attitudes is the trajectory of US-India relations, which have been far more turbulent than many in the community anticipated at the start of Trump's second term.
The White House has imposed a series of tariffs on India, citing trade barriers, the bilateral trade deficit and New Delhi's continued imports of Russian oil.
The Trump administration has also tightened restrictions on the H-1B visa programme, whose beneficiaries are predominantly Indian nationals. In recent months, anti-H-1B campaigns have gained traction in states such as Texas, targeting Indian companies and workers.
Critics of the programme have accused it of facilitating large-scale Indian immigration, displacing American workers and enabling visa fraud.
“There does appear to be growing dissatisfaction with President Trump among portions of the Indian American community,” Jani said.
“Some older Indian Americans who supported him may have anticipated a particularly strong US-India relationship given President Trump and Indian Prime Minister Modi’s personal relationship during Trump’s first term, while recent trade disputes and broader tensions in the bilateral relationship may have caused some of those voters to reassess that support.”
Dewan, who has worked on South Asian grassroots outreach for the presidential campaigns of Kamala Harris, Joe Biden, Hillary Clinton and Barack Obama, said she has encountered similar disappointment among some Indian Americans who supported Trump in 2024.
“In 2024, we met Indian Americans who voted for Trump because they believed his relationship with Modi would strengthen ties between the United States and India,” she said. “Two years later, some of those voters express regret.”
Immigration enforcement has emerged as another source of concern, according to Dewan.
“ICE detentions have reached families in the community, raising security concerns even among naturalized citizens,” she said. “Rising costs weigh on households, and so does the administration's more hostile posture toward India. For these reasons, some of these voters are returning to the community's traditional Democratic base.”
The immigration question
Yet political observers emphasise that Indian Americans are no longer a monolithic electorate. Although the community remains predominantly Democratic, survey findings reveal differences in political preferences based on age, gender and whether voters were born in the United States or abroad.
Jani pointed to a particularly notable divide: “US-born Indian American men have shown considerably greater openness to Republican candidates than other parts of the community.”
He also emphasised that views on immigration policy within the community are more nuanced than a simple partisan divide might suggest.
“Indian Americans may have a wide range of views on border security and illegal immigration, but rhetoric or enforcement perceived as indiscriminately anti-immigrant can resonate differently in a community where so many families have direct experience with the legal immigration system.”
While early voting figures offer clues about voter enthusiasm, political observers say a more significant development is the Indian American community's growing engagement in electoral politics, regardless of party affiliation.
Dewan captured that generational shift: “Twenty years ago, our parents wanted us to be doctors and engineers, not politicians. Today, they are knocking on doors for Indian American candidates running as Democrats and Republicans.”
